try: When you feel outnumbered today, say quietly: my protector is Allah. Then do the right thing.

title: They cannot help you. They cannot even help themselves.
subtitle: The helplessness of false gods

row.title: cannot defend itself
sub: so how can it defend you

then: Ibn Kathir tells of Amr ibn Al-Jamuh, a chief in Madinah who perfumed his idol. Two young men, both named Muadh, kept overturning it at night. He left a sword by it and said, defend yourself. When they tied it to a dead dog and threw it in a well, {trap}he realized it could not even save itself{/trap}, and {reward}he accepted Islam and held firm to it.{/reward}
now: You check the follower count, the salary, the savings, the right contact in your phone. {trap}You lean on them like they are holding you up.{/trap} {idea}Ask of each one: could it save itself?{/idea}
old: The things I rely on are strong enough to protect me.
new: Anything that cannot protect itself cannot truly protect me.
try: Pick one thing you lean on too hard. Say: this is from Allah, not my protector.

title: Eyes that look at you but do not see.
subtitle: Painted eyes, no sight
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the idols seem to face you but cannot see. {idea}The people who worship them are better than them{/idea}, because people hear, see and have strength. He cites Ibrahim asking his father, {trap}why worship what neither hears nor sees?{/trap}
now: You keep going back to the app for comfort after a hard day. It glows. It seems to look back. {trap}It does not know you exist.{/trap} {idea}You were made to turn to the One who sees you.{/idea}
old: Things that seem responsive must be meeting my needs.
new: Something can face me all day and still not see me. Allah sees me.
try: Tonight, put the phone face down for ten minutes and tell Allah about your day.

title: Forgive, call to good, walk away from fools.
subtitle: Three rules for dealing with people
then: Jibril explained this verse to the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}forgive those who wrong you, give to those who deprive you, keep ties with those who cut you.{/idea} Ibn Kathir tells how a man insulted Umar, who nearly punished him. His nephew recited this verse, and {reward}Umar did nothing more.{/reward}
now: Someone leaves a rude comment under your post. Your thumb is already typing the clever reply. {trap}You want the last word.{/trap} {idea}Close the app. Let the fool have the last word. You keep your peace.{/idea}
old: If I let rudeness pass, I look weak.
new: Pardoning and walking away is strength, not weakness.
try: The next time someone is rude today, say nothing back. Just wish them well inside.

title: When anger is stirred, run to Allah.
subtitle: The whisper that pushes you to retaliate
then: Right after the command to forgive, Allah warns about the urge that pulls against it. Ibn Jarir explains: {trap}if Shaytan lures you to anger, away from forgiving the ignorant and toward punishing him{/trap}, then seek refuge in Allah. Ibn Kathir notes a human enemy may soften with kindness, but {idea}the devil only leaves when you take refuge.{/idea}
now: Your sibling says the thing that always gets you. Your face heats up. Old fights replay in your head. {trap}That push is not only you.{/trap} {idea}Say a'udhu billah, take a breath, and step out of the room.{/idea}
old: My anger is completely mine. I just have to let it out.
new: Some of that push is a whisper, and I can ask Allah to shield me from it.
try: Next time you feel anger rising, say a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim before speaking.

title: They remember, and suddenly they see clearly.
subtitle: How the mindful recover
then: Ibn Kathir describes the people of taqwa: when an evil thought, anger, or the intention to do wrong crosses their mind, {idea}they remember Allah's punishment and His great reward{/idea}, repent and seek refuge. {reward}Then they see aright{/reward}, aware of the error of their ways.
now: You are halfway through typing the angry email. Then a verse you heard in Friday khutbah floats up. {idea}You stop.{/idea} {reward}Suddenly the email looks different. You delete it.{/reward}
old: Good people do not get bad thoughts.
new: The mindful get touched by bad thoughts too. They just remember quickly.
try: Choose one short dhikr to be your stop word today, and use it when a bad impulse shows up.

title: Their brothers keep pulling them deeper.
subtitle: The voices that never stop pushing
then: In contrast to the mindful, there are those Ibn Kathir calls {trap}the devils' brothers among mankind{/trap}, who follow and obey them. The devils make sin easy and appealing. Ibn Abbas said neither the people stop their evil nor do the devils stop luring them. {idea}The previous verse shows the way out.{/idea}
now: One episode becomes five. One bet becomes a weekly habit. One cigarette with friends becomes a pack. {trap}The push never gets tired.{/trap} {idea}You can still choose to be the person who remembers.{/idea}
old: I will stop once the pull gets weaker.
new: The pull does not get tired, so I have to step out myself.
try: Name one habit pulling you deeper. Put one small barrier in its way today.

title: Show us a miracle. This Book is the miracle.
subtitle: The demand for signs on demand
then: When the Prophet ﷺ did not bring a miracle, the pagans said: {trap}why have you not made one yourself?{/trap} He was told to answer that he only follows what his Lord reveals. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah then points to the Quran as {reward}the most powerful miracle and clearest proof{/reward}, guidance and mercy for those who believe.
now: You tell yourself you would be more religious if you could see some sign, a dream, a clear message. {trap}Meanwhile the app with the whole Quran sits unopened.{/trap} {idea}The sign you are waiting for is already in your hand.{/idea}
old: If I saw a real sign, I would change.
new: The Quran itself is the sign, and it is already here.
try: Read one page of the Quran today as if it were the sign you asked for.

title: When the Quran is recited, listen and be still.
subtitle: Silence as a door to mercy
then: After calling the Quran evidence, guidance and mercy, Allah commands people to listen to it in respect. Ibn Kathir notes this was the opposite of the Quraysh pagans, who said {trap}do not listen to this Quran, and make noise over it.{/trap} {reward}Listening in silence is a path to mercy.{/reward}
now: The Quran plays in the car while you argue on a call. It plays at the gathering while everyone talks over it. {trap}It becomes wallpaper.{/trap} {idea}Turn off everything else for one surah and actually hear it.{/idea}
old: Having the Quran on in the background is enough.
new: Mercy comes when I stop and truly listen.
try: Listen to one short surah today with nothing else going on. Eyes closed if you like.

title: Remember Him quietly, morning and evening.
subtitle: Inner dhikr, humble and close
then: Ibn Kathir notes this was revealed in Makkah before the five prayers were ordained. Travelers once raised their voices in dua, and the Prophet ﷺ told them {idea}you are not calling one who is deaf or absent, but One who hears and is near.{/idea} {trap}Do not be among the heedless.{/trap}
now: Morning: you check notifications before your feet touch the floor. Evening: you fall asleep mid-scroll. {trap}Allah is squeezed out at both ends.{/trap} {idea}A whispered subhanallah on the pillow reaches Him.{/idea}
old: Dhikr needs a special time and a loud voice to count.
new: A quiet, humble remembrance at dawn and dusk is close to Him.
try: Tomorrow morning, before touching your phone, say subhanallah quietly three times.

title: Those nearest to Him are never too proud to bow.
subtitle: The angels as a model for worship
then: The surah ends with the angels near Allah: {idea}they are never too proud to worship Him, they glorify Him and prostrate to Him.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says this reminder is so people imitate their tireless worship. He notes it is the first place in the Quran where reciters and listeners prostrate. {trap}Pride is what keeps a head up.{/trap}
now: You finish a big presentation. Everyone praises you. You feel tall. {trap}Prayer time comes and you push it back.{/trap} {idea}The ones closest to Allah never feel too big to put their forehead down.{/idea}
old: When I am doing well, I can let worship slide a little.
new: The closer I am to Allah, the more naturally I bow.
try: After your next success, make one sajdah of thanks to Allah.
